common_name: Anne Thomson Cranesbill (Golden-Leaved Magenta Trailing Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moderately fertile, free-draining but moisture-retentive soil in full sun to light shade; Anne Thomson spreads by trailing stems that root as they go, so give it room or a spot to cascade over a wall.

directions: A Geranium procurrens x psilostemon hybrid bred by Orkney geranium specialist Alan Bremner, Anne Thomson is grown for radiant chartreuse-gold foliage that sets off abundant magenta-pink flowers with a small black star at the center from midsummer into fall. It shares parentage with the better-known 'Ann Folkard' but stays more compact and holds up better in heat and humidity. The low, creeping mound roots as it spreads, making it a fast-covering groundcover or a striking cascade over a low wall.

common_name: Tiny Monster Cranesbill (Sterile Magenta-Pink Trailing Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, organic, free-draining soil in full sun to partial shade; being a sterile hybrid it puts no energy into seed production, so bloom is continuous rather than front-loaded.

directions: A German-raised cross of Geranium sanguineum and G. psilostemon, Tiny Monster is a ground-hugging, sterile hybrid that flowers almost continuously from late spring to early fall in large bright pink blooms veined in red. Because it sets no seed, its bloom energy carries through the whole season instead of tapering off after one main flush. The finely cut foliage spreads by trailing, non-invasive stems and turns rich scarlet in fall, giving it multi-season interest as a tough, low-maintenance groundcover.

common_name: Walter's Gift Cranesbill (Maroon-Marked Oxonianum Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in any moderately fertile, well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; foliage color develops best with a few hours of direct sun.

directions: Walter's Gift is grown as much for foliage as flower: its deeply lobed green leaves are boldly marked with dark maroon-red zones that intensify with more sun, creating a patterned mound even before bloom starts. From late spring to early autumn it produces pale pearly-pink flowers with darker veining above the marked foliage. Like other oxonianum cranesbills it is a reliable, easy-care clump former suited to mixed borders and groundcover duty. Divide every few years in spring to keep the patterning vivid and the clump vigorous.

common_name: Rose Clair Cranesbill (Heirloom Blush-to-Rose Oxonianum Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in any moderately fertile soil apart from waterlogged sites, in full sun or partial shade.

directions: A hybrid between Geranium endressii and G. versicolor, Rose Clair produces flowers that open nearly white and deepen through pale pink to a clear rose as they age, so the clump displays several shades of pink at once. Funnel-shaped, notched flowers with translucent veining appear from late spring into early autumn over a dome of dividing, ground-covering foliage. It asks for almost nothing beyond division every few years and tolerates a wide range of soils. Propagate by division in spring or basal cuttings taken in early to mid spring.

common_name: Katherine Adele Cranesbill (Maroon-Centered Foliage Oxonianum Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; the maroon foliage marking is most pronounced with some direct sun.

directions: Katherine Adele forms a broad mound of deeply lobed green leaves marked with dark maroon-burgundy patterning near the leaf center, giving the clump strong visual texture even between bloom flushes. From late spring to mid-autumn it bears pale pink-to-white flowers with darker purple veins above the patterned foliage. It is a dependable, long-blooming groundcover for mixed borders that combines well with hostas and ferns in part shade. Propagate by division in spring or basal cuttings rooted with bottom heat.

common_name: St. Ola Cranesbill (White-Flowered Cantabrigiense Groundcover Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun to full shade; St. Ola is unusually adaptable and tolerates both dry shade and damp ground once settled.

directions: A cross of Geranium dalmaticum with G. macrorrhizum 'Album', St. Ola forms a flat, dense mat of glossy foliage that turns antique red-orange in fall. In late spring and early summer it is covered in pure white flowers with pinkish veins and anthers that gradually age to a russet blush. Its flat, spreading habit and tolerance for both dry shade and damp soil make it one of the most versatile of the low cranesbill groundcovers, equally at home edging a woodland path or a sunny gravel bed.

common_name: Czakor Bigroot Geranium (Deep Magenta Macrorrhizum Groundcover)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in well-drained, average to poor soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; like the species, Czakor tolerates dry shade under mature trees better than nearly any other flowering groundcover.

directions: Czakor is a deeper-colored bigroot geranium selection bearing clusters of rich magenta flowers in late spring and early summer above the same aromatic, sticky, lobed foliage as the species. The scented leaves flush purple-red in autumn and resist deer and rabbit browsing year-round. It spreads steadily by surface rhizomes into a dense, weed-suppressing mat that is one of the most reliable groundcovers for the dry shade under mature trees and shrubs where little else thrives.

common_name: Shepherd's Warning Cranesbill (Dwarf Cerise-Pink Bloody Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, poor to average soil in full sun to partial shade; this dwarf form is ideal for rock gardens, troughs, and container culture.

directions: Shepherd's Warning is a genuinely dwarf bloody cranesbill, reaching only about 8 inches tall, with dense, low, dark foliage smothered in bright cerise-pink flowers from late spring into summer. Its compact scale suits rock gardens, troughs, and the front of a sunny border where larger sanguineum selections would overwhelm the space. Like the species it is drought-tolerant once established and needs no staking or coddling.

common_name: Mayflower Wood Cranesbill (Violet-Blue Sylvaticum Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to dappled sun in spring.

directions: A compact selection of wood cranesbill from Blooms of Bressingham, Mayflower bears rich violet-blue, saucer-shaped flowers with a small white center held above deeply divided foliage. It blooms earlier and more heavily than the straight species and performs best with consistent moisture, appreciating afternoon shade in hotter climates. It makes a strong companion for hostas and ferns in a woodland-edge border.

common_name: Album White Bigroot Geranium (Pure White Macrorrhizum Groundcover)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in well-drained, average to poor soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; once established it is highly drought tolerant, unusual for a groundcover geranium.

directions: Album is the white-flowered form of bigroot geranium, opening in late spring with blooms of white lightly blushed pale pink above the same aromatic, velvety, deeply lobed foliage as the species. It spreads slowly by surface rhizomes into a dense, semi-evergreen mat that tolerates dry shade under mature trees better than almost any flowering groundcover. The scented leaves are avoided by deer and rabbits and make Album a useful pale-color counterpoint to the magenta-pink species and its darker selections.

common_name: Elke Cranesbill (Fluorescent Pink White-Eyed Bloody Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light shade.

directions: A Belgian-raised bloody cranesbill selection, Elke bears large, vividly fluorescent pink flowers each marked with a bright white central pattern and a narrow white petal edge, blooming from late spring into autumn with a distinctive two-tone effect unlike other sanguineum cultivars. The bushy, semi-procumbent stems carry finely divided dark green leaves that trail attractively over edges and turn reddish in fall. It is adaptable across a wide range of conditions and performs well in containers as well as garden beds.

common_name: Oakington Blue Eyes Moss Phlox (Soft Lavender-Blue Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Plant container plants in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile to lean soil in full sun to partial shade; good drainage is essential to avoid crown rot.

directions: One of the older, vigorous classic moss phlox selections, Oakington Blue Eyes forms a low, dense cushion of dark green needle-like leaves that in mid-spring is completely covered in soft lavender-blue flowers, a gentler, cooler blue than the more purple-toned 'Emerald Blue'. It is exceptionally free-flowering and disease resistant, forming a tight, weed-suppressing evergreen mat through the rest of the year. Shear lightly after bloom to keep the mound dense, and site it in a sunny rock garden, wall crevice, or border edge where good drainage is guaranteed.

common_name: Wilhelm Kesselring Garden Phlox (Violet-Purple White-Eyed Tall Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing at least 18 inches apart for air circulation.

directions: A long-cultivated German garden phlox, Wilhelm Kesselring forms tall, dense, bushy clumps of lanceolate foliage topped from midsummer into early fall by fragrant violet-purple flower panicles with a small white eye. Its upright habit and reliable height make it well suited to the back of a border or as a solitary accent, and the fragrant blooms are good for cutting. Provide steady moisture and good air circulation in full sun to partial shade, and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Tenor Garden Phlox (Rich Magenta-Red Tall Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing for good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew.

directions: Tenor is an early-blooming garden phlox with strong, sturdy stems that carry large, rounded clusters of rich magenta-red flowers accented by a darker red eye, creating a starry, fragrant display from midsummer into early fall. Its compact, upright habit and early bloom timing set it apart from later-flowering red-toned cultivars, and the fragrant flowers draw butterflies and hummingbirds while excelling as cut flowers. Deadhead spent panicles to prolong bloom and cut plants back in late autumn.

common_name: Grenadine Dream Garden Phlox (Compact Fragrant Reddish-Pink Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; the stiff stems of Grenadine Dream rarely need staking.

directions: Grenadine Dream is a compact, conical garden phlox holding densely packed, fragrant reddish-purple flower clusters over an unusually long bloom period from July into October. Its tight, upright habit on stiff stems means it rarely needs staking, unlike many taller Phlox paniculata cultivars. Deadhead to extend flowering and site in full sun to partial shade with even moisture for the best display.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center Phlox Trial Garden Report

common_name: Blue Boy Garden Phlox (Historic Mauve-Blue Tall Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; older cultivars like Blue Boy are more prone to powdery mildew and benefit from generous air circulation.

directions: One of the classic older garden phlox cultivars, Blue Boy is valued for flowers that shift from bluish mauve with a whitish center in bright sun to a noticeably softer, bluer lavender in the low light of evening. It blooms relatively late in the season on tall stems and attracts butterflies and hummingbirds. As an older selection it is more susceptible to powdery mildew than modern resistant cultivars, so give it full sun, even moisture, and plenty of airflow.

common_name: Marjorie Moss Phlox (Rose-Pink Cerise-Marked Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Plant container plants in late winter or early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Marjorie tolerates light dappled shade better than most moss phlox selections.

directions: Marjorie is a classic rock-garden moss phlox forming a low, dense evergreen mound of needle-like foliage that in late spring produces a profusion of star-shaped, rose-pink flowers, each petal marked at the base with a small cerise paintbrush stroke. It is more tolerant of light dappled shade than many subulata selections while still flowering heavily in full sun. Use it to trail over the edge of a raised bed or dry wall, or as a front-of-border carpet, shearing lightly after bloom to keep growth tight.

common_name: Nettleton Variation Moss Phlox (Variegated Salmon-Pink Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Plant container plants in late winter or early spring in well-drained, gritty soil in full sun to light shade; the variegated foliage is the main draw and stays showy through the cool season.

directions: A sport of 'Alexander's Surprise' found by a UK nurseryman, Nettleton Variation is grown chiefly for its foliage: cream-margined needle-like leaves that flush pink in cold weather, giving winter and early-spring interest most moss phlox lack. In spring it is topped with clusters of salmon-pink flowers, but the variegated evergreen mat remains the year-round attraction. Give it gritty, well-drained soil and use it as an accent groundcover in a rock garden or trough where the foliage color can be appreciated up close.

common_name: Jade Garden Phlox (White Green-Edged Bicolor Tall Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: A distinctive bicolor garden phlox from Dutch breeding, Jade bears fragrant, pure white flowers edged in pale celadon green, giving the flower clusters a cool, subtle two-tone effect unlike the pink- or magenta-eyed white cultivars common in the genus. It is noted for good mildew resistance and petals that hold on the stem rather than dropping, making it a strong choice for cut-flower use. Grow in fertile, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade for the best flower display.

common_name: Amethyst Garden Phlox (Color-Changing Purple Tall Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in fertile, evenly moist soil in full sun for the best flower color and mildew resistance.

directions: Amethyst is one of the so-called 'changeling' garden phlox, its broad, rounded flower clusters reading as a medium purple in daytime sun but deepening to a richer, more saturated purple at dusk, dawn, and on overcast days. Unopened flower buds are white, adding contrast to the clusters before they open fully. It is noted for good resistance to powdery mildew relative to many older paniculata cultivars and attracts butterflies and hummingbirds through its long summer bloom.
